questions.los: Choosing a model when dividends exceed FCFE
questions.stem: Which of the following valuation models is most appropriate for Firm A?

explanations.A: A is correct because Firm A is planning significant expansion, which will result in dividends exceeding free cash flow to equity. Generally, defining returns as free cash flow and using the FCFE (and FCFF) models are most suitable when the company is dividend-paying but dividends significantly exceed or fall short of free cash flow to equity.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because the residual income model relies on the quality of accounting to be good, so that an analyst can appropriately adjust net income and book value. If the quality of accounting disclosure is good, the analyst may be able to calculate residual income by making appropriate adjustments (to reported net income and book value, in particular). In some cases, the degree of distortion and the quality of accounting disclosure can be such that the application of the residual income model is error-prone.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because Firm A is planning to maintain dividend payments at pre-expansion levels, regardless of future profitability. The DDM is most suitable when the board of directors has established a dividend policy that bears an understandable and consistent relationship to the company’s profitability. The fact that the dividend payout ratio has been stable for the last 10 years is not relevant going forward.

questions.los: Multi-year DDM with terminal price; fair-value band
questions.stem: Based on the dividend discount model, Bala should consider Firm B’s common stock to be:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because the current share price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above the fair value of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.
explanations.B: B is correct because the value of Firm B’s stock is the present value of the expected dividends for the next three years plus the present value of the expected price at the end of Year 3. V0 = D1/(1 + r)1 + D2/(1 + r)2 + D3/(1 + r)3 + P3/(1 + r)3 where: D1 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 1; D2 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 2; D3 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 3; P3 = expected price at the end of Year 3 = $21.50; r = required return on equity = 8.0%. Given a dividend payout ratio of 40% (= 1 – retention ratio = 1 – 60%), D1 = EPS1 × dividend payout ratio = $1.27 × 40% = $0.51; D2 = EPS2 × dividend payout ratio = $1.62 × 40% = $0.65; D3 = EPS3 × dividend payout ratio = $1.91 × 40% = $0.76. V0 = $0.51/(1.08)1 + $0.65/(1.08)2 + $0.76/(1.08)3 + $21.50/(1.08)3 = $18.70. The current share price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above this estimate of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the current price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above the fair value of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: V0 = Σ Dt/(1+r)^t + P3/(1+r)^3; Dt = EPSt × payout ratio; payout = 1 – retention = 40%

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: V0 = $18.70; price $19.00 is 1.6% above → within 2% band → fairly valued

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Payout = 1 – retention (40%), not 60%; the $19.00 vs $18.70 gap (1.6%) is inside the 2% fair-value band.

questions.los: Sustainable growth rate via DuPont (g = b × ROE)
questions.stem: Based on the DuPont model, the sustainable growth rate for Firm C is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because the sustainable growth rate is the rate of dividend (and earnings) growth that can be sustained for a given level of return on equity, assuming that the capital structure is constant through time and that additional common stock is not issued. Based on the DuPont model, the sustainable growth rate can be expressed as a function of profit margin, retention rate, asset turnover, and financial leverage: g = (1 – Dividend Payout Ratio) × Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × (Total Assets/Equity). For Firm C, g = (1 – 45%) × 11.5% × 0.65 × 2.25 = 9.25%

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: g = retention rate × ROE, with ROE via DuPont = net profit margin × asset turnover × (assets/equity)

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Retention = 1 – payout (0.55); multiply all three DuPont components for ROE before applying retention.

questions.los: Gordon growth sensitivity when r and g rise equally
questions.stem: Under Bala's sensitivity scenario, Firm C's estimated share price is expected to:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because, although the spread between the cost of equity and the earnings growth rate remains constant, next year’s dividend will increase, thereby resulting in a higher estimated stock price.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because the formula for valuing a firm's common stock with the Gordon growth model is V0 = D0 × (1 + g) / (r – g), where D0 = dividend just paid; g = expected constant growth rate in dividends (or earnings); r = cost of equity. So, if the numerator goes up (g increases) while the denominator stays the same (both r and g increase by the same amount), V0 increases.

questions.los: Credit analysis approaches for a granular homogeneous ABS
questions.stem: Based on the characteristics of the receivables backing the ABS, which credit analysis approach is most appropriate?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because a loan-by-loan approach is more appropriate for non-granular, heterogeneous portfolios. The ABS in the fund portfolio is homogeneous and granular because there are many relatively small receivables in the pool. A loan-by-loan approach would be inefficient because of the large number of basically similar loans.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. If the risk horizon were medium-term, a portfolio-based approach would be more appropriate because the portfolio is not static but changes over time.
explanations.C: C is correct because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. The credit card ABS is granular, with many small loans relative to the size of the total portfolio. The credit card receivables are also homogeneous, and the risk horizon is short-term. Investors in this type of ABS will base their probability of default on the mean default probability, recovery rate, and variance of a portfolio of borrowers reflecting the distribution of FICO scores within the pool rather than conducting an analysis of individual borrowers. These statistics are sufficient to gauge the key credit metrics of the loan pool and therefore point to a statistics-based approach for credit analysis.

questions.los: Expected 1-year total return under a transition matrix
questions.stem: Based on the 1-year corporate transition matrix, the expected 1-year total return on the Valisker bond is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because the expected return on the bond over the next year is its YTM minus the expected percentage change in the bond value over the year. First, we must calculate the expected percentage price change for each possible transition as the product of the modified duration and the change in the spread: From AA to AAA: –2.82 × (0.65% – 0.95%) = +0.846%; From AA to A: –2.82 × (1.20% – 0.95%) = –0.705%; From AA to BBB: –2.82 × (1.80% – 0.95%) = –2.397%; From AA to BB: –2.82 × (3.60% – 0.95%) = –7.473%. The probabilities of migration can now be used to calculate the expected percentage change in the bond value over the year. The expected percentage change in bond value for an AA-rated corporate bond is found by multiplying each expected percentage price change by its respective credit transition probability found in the row associated with the AA rating and summing the products: (0.02 × 0.846%) + (0.88 × 0%) + (0.08 × –0.705%) + (0.014 × –2.397%) + (0.006 × –7.473%) = –0.11788%. Therefore, the expected return on the bond over the next year is its YTM minus 0.11788%: 2.60% – 0.11788% = 2.48212% ~ 2.48%.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Expected return = YTM + Σ [ (–ModDur × Δspread) × probability ] using the AA-rating row

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Δspread is measured from the current AA spread (0.95%); staying AA (prob 0.88) has 0% change; add YTM back.

questions.stem: The upfront premium the fund would receive for purchasing the CDS protection on Gonk Industries is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because an approximation for the upfront premium is (Credit spread – Fixed coupon rate) × Duration of the CDS. To buy 5-year CDS protection, an investor would have to pay a 500 bps coupon plus the present value of the difference between that coupon and the current market spread (400 bps). In this case, the upfront premium is approximately: Upfront premium % ≈ (Credit spread – Fixed coupon) × Duration = (4.0% – 5.0%) × 4.5 = –4.5%. The upfront premium is then converted to a dollar value: Upfront premium % × Notional = –4.5% × $5,000,000 = –$225,000. Because the company’s credit spread is less than the fixed coupon, the protection seller must pay the upfront premium to the protection buyer.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Upfront premium % ≈ (credit spread – fixed coupon) × CDS duration; then × notional

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = –$225,000 (negative → protection buyer RECEIVES it because spread < coupon)

steps.label: 陷阱

questions.stem: The cash settlement amount for the fund from the Gonk Industries CDS is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the cheapest-to-deliver, or lowest-priced, instrument is the 7-year senior unsecured bond trading at 30% of par. Although the 3-year bond trades at a lower price, it is subordinated and, therefore, does not qualify for coverage under the CDS. Note that, even though the reference bond for the CDS is the 5-year bond, the fund will receive payment on the CDS based on the cheapest-to-deliver obligation regardless of maturity. Any debt obligation issued by the borrower that is ranked equal to or higher than the reference obligation with respect to the priority of claims is covered. Loss given default (LGD) = 1 – Recovery rate (%) = 1 – 30% = 70%. Payout amount = LGD × Notional = 70% × $5,000,000 = $3,500,000.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: CTD eligible = 7-year senior at 30% of par (the 3-year at 20% is subordinated → ineligible); LGD = 1 – 30% = 70%

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: The subordinated 3-year bond (20%) is cheaper but ranks below the reference obligation, so it does not qualify; use the 7-year senior at 30%.

questions.los: Cointegration: unit-root tests on two series plus Engle-Granger test on regression residuals
questions.stem: The time series ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) are cointegrated if the tests performed by Silva:

choices.C: fail to reject all three null hypotheses.

explanations.A: Correct. To be cointegrated, two time series must both have a unit root (fail to reject Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 by a Dickey-Fuller test) AND the residuals of the regression between them must not have a unit root (reject Null Hypothesis 3 by an Engle-Granger Dickey-Fuller test). Only this scenario (both series have a unit root and the error term of the regression does not) corresponds to cointegration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rejecting Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 would mean neither series has a unit root, so they cannot be cointegrated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failing to reject Null Hypothesis 3 means the regression error term has a unit root, so the series are not cointegrated (Scenario 5).

questions.stem: The mean-reverting level of dln(PRIVt) is closest to:

explanations.B: Correct. The mean-reverting level of the dependent variable of an AR(1) model is b0/(1 - b1) = 0.00259/(1 - 0.38616) = 0.0042.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.387 is the slope coefficient b1, not the mean-reverting level.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Mean-reverting level = b0 / (1 - b1)

steps.label: Trap
steps.content: Do not report b0 (0.002) or b1 (0.387) directly.

questions.los: ARCH(1) test: regress squared residuals on one lag of squared residuals
questions.stem: Do the estimates of the residual regression parameters indicate that the AR(1) model on dln(PUBLt) is misspecified?

choices.B: Yes, because there is evidence of significant serial correlation
choices.C: Yes, because there is evidence of autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Residual Regression 2 indicates the model exhibits ARCH, hence it is not well specified.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no evidence of significant serial correlation: the slope of Residual Regression 1 (t = 0.70) is not statistically different from 0, so we cannot reject the null that the residuals are not autocorrelated.
explanations.C: Correct. Engle's test regresses the squared residuals on a constant and one lag of the squared residuals (et^2 = a0 + a1*et-1^2 + ut); if a1 is significant the series is ARCH(1). For Residual Regression 2 the t-statistic on a1 is 2.94 > critical value 1.97, so the model exhibits ARCH and is misspecified.

questions.los: Feature selection for text data: mutual information
questions.stem: To perform feature selection, Silva should select the tokens with the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tokens with the lowest term frequency are likely noise features, which Silva wants to remove, not select.
explanations.B: Correct. Mutual information measures how much information a token contributes to a class of text. Tokens that occur more often in a particular class have high MI; selecting the highest-MI tokens keeps the informative features and removes noise.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Highest document frequency tends to identify very common tokens that appear across all classes and carry little discriminating information.

questions.los: Algorithm selection: SVM soft margin for non-linear separability without overfitting
questions.stem: Which of the following machine-learning algorithms is most suitable for Moreno's bond issuer classification model?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Non-linear SVM introduces more complex non-linear separation boundaries; it may reduce training misclassifications but is more complex and prone to overfitting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An unconstrained CART makes no assumptions about the training data and can perfectly learn (overfit) it; avoiding overfitting requires regularization such as maximum depth or minimum node population.
explanations.C: Correct. SVM with soft margin classification handles non-linear separability by adding a penalty to the objective function for misclassified training observations, optimizing the trade-off between a wider margin and a lower total error penalty, and is less prone to overfitting.

questions.los: Adding a variable: R^2 and adjusted R^2 behavior (t-stat rule of |1.0|)
questions.stem: Compared to Model 2, Model 3 most likely has a:

choices.A: lower R-squared and a higher adjusted R-squared.
choices.B: higher R-squared and a lower adjusted R-squared.
choices.C: higher R-squared and a higher adjusted R-squared.

explanations.A: Incorrect. R-squared cannot decrease when a variable is added.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adjusted R-squared decreases only if the added variable's t-statistic is below |1.0|; here QUICK has t = 1.9204 > 1.0.
explanations.C: Correct. As independent variables are added, R-squared increases or stays the same. Adjusted R-squared rises if the new coefficient's t-statistic exceeds |1.0| and falls if it is below |1.0|. QUICK's t-statistic is 1.9204, so adjusted R-squared for Model 3 is higher than for Model 2.

questions.los: Conditional heteroskedasticity from residual plot; effect on F-test reliability
questions.stem: The most appropriate conclusion to draw from the residual plot for Model 4 is that:

choices.A: the model suffers from unconditional heteroskedasticity.
choices.B: there is a non-linear relationship between ROE and SALES.
choices.C: the F-test for the overall regression significance is unreliable.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unconditional heteroskedasticity occurs when the error variance is NOT correlated with the independent variables and creates no major inference problems. Here the residual variance rises with SALES, so the variance is correlated with the regressor -- this is conditional, not unconditional, heteroskedasticity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plot of residuals against a feature does not reveal the nature of the target-feature relationship; the pattern here is about error variance, not non-linearity.
explanations.C: Correct. The residual variance increases with SALES, i.e., the error variance is conditional on the regressor -- conditional heteroskedasticity. This makes the MSE a biased estimator of the true population variance, so the F-test for overall regression significance is unreliable, and it tends to find significant relationships where none exist (more Type I errors).

questions.los: Model evaluation: recall minimizes false negatives (Type II errors)
questions.stem: Which machine-learning model should Aoun choose given his concern about false negatives?

explanations.A: Correct. Recall is the ratio of correctly predicted positives to all actual positives and is the metric to maximize when the cost of false negatives (Type II errors) is high. Model X has the highest recall (0.94 vs 0.90 and 0.82).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Accuracy and F1 score (highest for Model Y) weight false positives and negatives equally; they do not directly address the higher cost of false negatives.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Precision (highest for Model Z) addresses the cost of false positives (Type I errors), the opposite of Aoun's concern.

questions.los: ARCH(1): error variance is time-varying but predictable from prior squared error
questions.stem: Based on Aoun's conclusion regarding the time-series model for Bytewave, the variance of the error term is:

explanations.A: Correct. With ARCH(1) errors, the variance of the error in period t+1 can be predicted in period t because it depends on how large the squared error was in the previous period. Thus the error variance is predictable but not constant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ARCH errors are by definition not constant (the variance changes with the prior squared error).
explanations.C: Incorrect. ARCH(1) errors are predictable: the variance depends linearly on the previous period's squared error.

questions.los: Covariance stationarity: constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance
questions.stem: The first-differenced time series for Circuitcraft's growth in quarterly sales:

explanations.A: Incorrect. In a random walk the best forecast of xt is xt-1. Here b2 = -0.5272 with t = -4.3411 (|t| > 2.0), so b2 is significant and its absolute value is less than 1; xt-1 is not the best forecast in every subsequent period, so the series is not a random walk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Seasonality would show a significant fourth (quarterly) residual autocorrelation. The largest residual autocorrelation t-statistic is 1.8424 (lag 3) < 2.0, so no autocorrelation differs significantly from 0 and there is no seasonality.
explanations.C: Correct. None of the residual autocorrelations differ significantly from 0 (largest |t| = 1.8424 < 2.0), so the autocovariance is constant. Aoun determines the mean and variance are constant over time. All three requirements of a covariance-stationary series (constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance) are satisfied.

questions.stem: Which of the following machine learning algorithms is most appropriate for Cambo to use when selecting the stocks for the new ETF?

explanations.A: Correct. Agglomerative (bottom-up hierarchical) clustering treats each observation as its own cluster, then iteratively combines the two closest clusters by a similarity measure. Grouping stocks by co-movement similarity of returns with an unknown number of groups is unsupervised learning, making agglomerative clustering the appropriate choice.

questions.los: Breusch-Pagan test for conditional heteroskedasticity (one-tail chi-square)
questions.stem: If Cambo assumes a significance level of 5%, based on the result of the BP test he should conclude that the:

choices.A: statistics of the independent variables are unreliable.
choices.B: residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Because the null is not rejected, the model does not have conditional heteroskedasticity and there is no basis to call the statistics unreliable.
explanations.B: Correct. The Breusch-Pagan test is a one-tail (right-tail) chi-square test with k = 3 degrees of freedom; at the 5% level the critical value is 7.815. Because the BP statistic 5.8 < 7.815, the null is not rejected: the residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity and the standard errors are unbiased.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Underestimated standard errors would arise if conditional heteroskedasticity were present; here it is not detected.

questions.stem: What type of error appears to be present in Exhibit 1?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An invalidity error is data outside a meaningful range; that is not the issue here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An inconsistency error is a data point conflicting with another; that is not what is shown.
explanations.C: Correct. A non-uniformity error occurs when data are not presented in an identical format. The Date of Birth column mixes formats, and the Salary column uses an ambiguous dollar symbol (US dollar, Canadian dollar, or others).

questions.los: Classification errors: Type I error (false positive) at the chosen threshold
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the most appropriate statement about the model's performance for the selected credit applicant is that it results in:

explanations.A: Correct. The threshold p-value for Class 1 (default) is 0.6 and the applicant's p = 0.65 meets it, so the model predicts default (Class 1). The actual outcome is non-default (Class 0), so the loan is misclassified as likely to default -- a Type I error (false positive).
explanations.B: Incorrect. A Type II error (false negative) would be predicting non-default when the applicant actually defaults; the opposite happened.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The prediction (default) does not match the actual outcome (non-default), so it is not a correct classification.

questions.los: AR model specification: significant residual autocorrelation implies misspecification
questions.stem: Model A is most likely:

choices.B: misspecified based on the statistical results observed in the model's residuals.
choices.C: misspecified based on the coefficient of the first lag.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Significant residual autocorrelation at the second lag indicates the model is not correctly specified.
explanations.B: Correct. The AR(1) model is misspecified because of the significant autocorrelation of the residuals at the second lag; an additional lag should be added.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The significant first-lag coefficient is expected in an AR(1) and does not by itself indicate misspecification; the residual autocorrelation does.

questions.los: Dickey-Fuller test: reject H0(g1=0) implies stationary (no unit root)
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 3, the test that Lin conducts for model A:

choices.B: indicates that model A is stationary.
choices.C: indicates that model A exhibits a unit root.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The result is conclusive: the null is clearly rejected.
explanations.B: Correct. The Dickey-Fuller test uses Xt - Xt-1 = b0 + g1*Xt-1 + et with H0: g1 = 0 (unit root, nonstationary) vs Ha: g1 < 0 (no unit root, stationary). The t-statistic of 10.542 with p-value 0.000 rejects the null, indicating the series is stationary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A unit root corresponds to failing to reject H0; here H0 is rejected.

explanations.C: Incorrect. The call itself has positive gamma, but because Wu is short the call, her position's gamma is negative, not positive.

questions.los: Reverse carry arbitrage when observed forward price is below fair value
questions.stem: Exploiting the arbitrage opportunity in Reyab shares involves:

choices.B: selling the forward contract and investing the proceeds at the risk-free interest rate.
choices.C: buying the forward contract, selling the underlying short, and investing the proceeds at the risk-free interest rate.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Selling the forward and buying the underlying with borrowed funds (carry arbitrage) is appropriate when the observed forward price is ABOVE the arbitrage-free price, which is not the case here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Selling the forward and investing proceeds leaves the investor exposed to price risk and is not an arbitrage.
explanations.C: Correct. The observed forward price (63.25) is below the arbitrage-free price (63.65), so reverse carry arbitrage applies: buy the forward, sell the underlying short, and lend (invest) the short-sale proceeds at the risk-free rate.

questions.los: Fund of funds vs multi-strategy fund: leverage, fee layers, reaction time
questions.stem: Compared to Option 2, Option 1 most likely has:

explanations.A: Correct. Multi-strategy funds (Option 2) tend to use significantly more leverage than most funds of funds (Option 1), which gravitate to modest leverage. So the fund of funds most likely has less leverage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A fund of funds typically has a double layer of fees, whereas in a multi-strategy fund fee netting is handled at the strategy level. The fund of funds has more, not fewer, fee layers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because a fund of funds executes strategies across different underlying funds, it has a slower (longer) tactical reaction time than a multi-strategy fund.

questions.los: Appraisal-based index: appraisal lag smooths returns (understated volatility)
questions.stem: Friso's choice of real estate index will most likely result in:

choices.C: higher correlation of returns with the rest of the portfolio.

explanations.A: Correct. An appraisal-based index smooths returns and understates volatility because of the appraisal lag (many properties are not appraised every quarter, so index information is out of date), which is especially pronounced during sudden market shifts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The smoothing lowers volatility and therefore overstates, not underestimates, the Sharpe ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The appraisal lag smooths the index and gives it a lower, not higher, correlation with other asset classes.

questions.los: REIT vs REOC: distribution requirements and dividend payout
questions.stem: Compared to Rainfall Real Estate, Perpetua Properties most likely has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. As a REIT, Perpetua benefits from tax exemptions (it can deduct dividends paid), effectively exempting it from corporate income tax in many countries, so it does not have a higher effective tax rate.
explanations.B: Correct. As a REIT, Perpetua must distribute 90-100% of its taxable income to shareholders, whereas the REOC (Rainfall) can retain earnings. Therefore Perpetua most likely has a higher dividend payout ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. REITs must distribute 90-100% of taxable earnings and have little retained earnings for growth. REOCs, with fewer restrictions and no distribution requirement, have greater flexibility to retain earnings.

questions.los: AFFO as the best measure of a REIT's sustainable dividend-paying capacity
questions.stem: Which of the following measures of income would best meet Friso's key objective in her analysis of Perpetua Properties?

explanations.A: Incorrect. FFO is not a cash flow measure; it excludes the investment and spending needed to sustain cash flow growth and cash flow from financing activities.
explanations.B: Correct. AFFO (funds/cash available for distribution) is a more accurate, cash-focused measure of sustainable economic income than FFO or net income; it considers the capital expenditures needed to maintain the property portfolio and is more reflective of a REIT's dividend-paying ability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Net income includes many non-cash charges and estimates, so it is not a good measure of a REIT's dividend-paying capacity.

choices.B: No, they fail to meet Requirement 1

explanations.A: Correct. Liquid alts most likely meet both requirements. They typically do not charge incentive fees (in most countries liquid alts are prohibited from charging one), meeting Requirement 1, and they offer daily redemption rights, more frequent than traditional hedge funds, meeting Requirement 2.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liquid alts typically have no incentive fee, so they meet Requirement 1.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liquid alts offer daily redemptions -- greater liquidity than traditional hedge funds -- so they meet Requirement 2.

questions.los: Multi-strategy fund vs fund of funds: returns, leverage, redemption gates
questions.stem: Compared to Strategy 2, Strategy 1 most likely has:

explanations.A: Correct. Multi-strategy funds (Strategy 1) have generally outperformed funds of funds (Strategy 2), though with more variance and occasional large losses tied to higher leverage; their advantage comes from flexibility and fast tactical asset allocation within a single fund structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multi-strategy funds tend to use significantly more, not less, leverage than funds of funds.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multi-strategy funds often impose investor- or fund-level gates on maximum quarterly redemptions, so they do not have fewer gates.

questions.los: Long/short equity: stock selection as the primary source of manager skill
questions.stem: Which factor is most likely the primary source of outperformance for the Strategy 3 manager?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Most long/short equity managers time markets poorly (too net long at highs, not net long enough at lows); market timing is secondary at best.
explanations.B: Correct. Stock selection defines manager skill for most long/short equity managers, with market-timing ability an additive but generally secondary consideration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leverage can amplify positions (used mostly by quantitative managers), but it is not the primary source of skill; stock selection is.

questions.los: Strategy best suited to limit drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio
questions.stem: Which of the following hedge fund strategies is best suited to meet the plan's drawdown objective?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Event-driven/distressed strategies show high maximum drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio and provide little risk reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. When combined with a traditional stock and bond portfolio, opportunistic strategies -- specifically global macro and systematic futures (as well as merger arbitrage and equity market-neutral) -- generate the smallest maximum drawdowns and have low serial autocorrelation (good liquidity), providing risk mitigation even during market stress.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Relative value/convertible arbitrage strategies show high maximum drawdowns and relatively high standard deviations when combined with the traditional portfolio, offering little risk-reduction benefit.

explanations.B: Correct. Under the neoclassical model the steady-state growth rate = TFP growth scaled by the labor share plus labor force growth: 2.1%/0.552 + 0.9% = 3.804% + 0.9% = 4.70%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5.6% adds labor productivity growth (3.5%) rather than correctly scaling TFP growth by the labor share.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Steady-state growth = theta/(1 - alpha) + n, where 1 - alpha = labor share = 0.552

questions.los: Labor productivity growth accounting: potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth
questions.stem: Based on the labor productivity growth accounting equation, the potential GDP growth rate of Country B is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2.0% omits part of the sum.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth in potential GDP = growth in the labor force + growth in labor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% = 2.8%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.3% double counts by adding TFP growth on top of labor productivity growth.

steps.label: Formula

questions.los: Endogenous growth model: open trade permanently raises the growth rate
questions.stem: Which of the following models would best support Podlasky's conclusion regarding the impact of removing Country A's trade barriers?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The classical model does not predict a permanent increase in per capita growth from open trade.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In the neoclassical model open trade raises the level of output and speeds convergence but does not permanently raise the growth rate.
explanations.C: Correct. Open trade fosters innovation and, through selection, scale, and backwardness effects, endogenous growth models predict that a more open trade policy will permanently raise the rate of economic growth, matching Podlasky's conclusion of a permanent increase in per capita growth.

questions.los: Output gap implications for long-term equity returns and short-term inflation
questions.stem: Podlasky's revisions to the growth forecasts for Country B most likely imply:

choices.A: lower expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.
choices.B: higher expected long-term equity returns and lower expected short-term inflation.
choices.C: higher expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A higher growth rate in potential GDP implies higher, not lower, long-term equity returns.
explanations.B: Correct. A higher estimated growth rate in potential GDP implies higher long-term equity returns, and a lower estimate of short-term GDP growth (below potential) puts downward pressure on inflation, implying lower expected short-term inflation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Short-term GDP growth below potential puts downward, not upward, pressure on inflation, so expected short-term inflation is lower.

questions.los: Triangular arbitrage: compare dealer cross rate with interbank implied cross rate
questions.stem: Based on the dealer's JPY/EUR quote, is there an arbitrage opportunity for the hedge fund?

choices.B: Yes, by purchasing EUR in the interbank market and selling EUR to the dealer
choices.C: Yes, by purchasing EUR from the dealer and selling EUR in the interbank market

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is an arbitrage: the dealer's EUR offer is cheaper than the interbank implied bid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the profitable trade; buying EUR interbank and selling to the dealer would lose money.
explanations.C: Correct. The interbank implied JPY/EUR is 119.4342/119.5550 (USD/EUR times JPY/USD). The dealer quotes 119.38/119.40, so the fund can buy EUR from the dealer at 119.40 and sell EUR in the interbank market at 119.43 for a profit.

questions.los: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
questions.stem: Based on covered interest rate parity, the 6-month forward USD/NZD exchange rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.6774 has the interest-rate ratio inverted.
explanations.B: Correct. F(USD/NZD) = S0 * (1 + rUS/2)/(1 + rNZD/2) = 0.6808 * (1 + 0.005/2)/(1 + 0.01/2) = 0.6791. Because NZD has the higher interest rate, it trades at a forward discount.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.6825 applies the rate differential in the wrong direction, implying a forward premium for the higher-yielding currency.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: F(f/d) = S(f/d) * (1 + i(price)/2)/(1 + i(base)/2) for a 6-month tenor

questions.los: Warning signs of a currency crisis: FX reserves decline relative to FX turnover
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions would most likely be a warning sign of a currency crisis in Country B?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Large inflows of foreign capital typically precede a crisis; Country B shows a slight decline in foreign investment, not an inflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Broad money growth and the ratio of M2 to bank reserves tend to rise before a crisis; here these indicators have declined.
explanations.C: Correct. Foreign exchange reserves tend to decline precipitously as a crisis approaches. The sizable decline in the ratio of FX reserves to average daily FX turnover is the warning sign present in Country B.

questions.los: Growth accounting (Cobb-Douglas): output growth = TFP + alpha*capital growth + (1-alpha)*labor growth
questions.stem: Based on the information given to Team Blue, the estimate of the economy's potential growth rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Correct. Growth accounting: output growth = TFP growth + alpha*capital growth + (1 - alpha)*labor growth = 1.0% + 0.30*2.0% + 0.70*0.5% = 1.0% + 0.6% + 0.35% = 1.95%.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 2.55% mis-weights capital and labor (for example, applying full weights).
explanations.C: Incorrect. 3.50% sums the raw factor growth rates without applying the income shares.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Output growth = TFP + alpha*(capital growth) + (1 - alpha)*(labor growth), alpha = 0.30

questions.los: Capital deepening, TFP measurement, and investment's link to the existing capital stock
questions.stem: Which of the points raised by Team Green is most likely correct?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The relationship between growth and R&D spending is not clear-cut: technological innovation raises output in the long run but can cause cyclical slowing through creative destruction (the double-edged nature of innovation).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The statement is reversed: labor productivity growth equals the contribution of capital deepening plus TFP; capital deepening is measured as the difference between labor productivity growth and TFP growth.
explanations.C: Correct. Although long-term sustainable growth cannot rely on pure capital deepening, the impact of investment spending on available capital depends on the existing physical capital stock, which explains the strong cross-country correlation between investment spending and economic growth (the effect is especially large in developing countries with low capital per worker).

questions.los: Convergence concepts: human-capital externalities imply non-convergence
questions.stem: Which of the following convergence concepts is most compatible with Team Purple's conclusion?

explanations.A: Correct. Emphasizing the externalities associated with human capital implies a linear (straight-line) production function and is compatible with non-convergence: the endogenous growth model makes no prediction that convergence should occur, allowing high-income countries with more capital to stay ahead through high rates of investment in knowledge and human capital.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Absolute convergence assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital, which is inconsistent with strong human-capital externalities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conditional convergence also assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital (conditional on the same saving rate, population growth, and production function), inconsistent with the emphasis on human-capital externalities.

questions.los: Capital flows and convergence: adjustment dynamics under open trade
questions.stem: Which of the following descriptions provided by Team Orange is consistent with Smith's conclusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. During the transition, growth in the capital-exporting (developed) countries will be below, not above, the steady state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because capital flows are matched by offsetting trade flows, developed countries that export capital will tend to run trade surpluses, not deficits.
explanations.C: Correct. Developing countries have less capital per worker and a higher marginal product of capital, so the rate of return on investments is higher in low capital-to-labor countries and lower in countries with high capital-to-labor ratios, consistent with Smith's conclusion.

questions.los: Endogenous growth model: constant returns to capital (no diminishing returns)
questions.stem: Which of the following is not true according to the endogenous growth model?

choices.A: The economy does not converge to a steady-state rate of growth.
choices.B: Increasing capital will result in diminishing marginal returns.
choices.C: Spending on R&D has positive externalities that benefit the whole economy.

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e., this statement is true). In the endogenous growth model the economy does not converge to a steady-state rate of growth.
explanations.B: Correct (this is the untrue statement). Unlike the neoclassical model, which assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital, endogenous growth models assume investment in capital can have constant returns, so increasing the saving rate can permanently raise the growth rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e., this statement is true). R&D spending has positive externalities that benefit the whole economy, a key feature of the endogenous growth model.

questions.los: Mundell-Fleming: both expansionary policies leave the currency effect indeterminate
questions.stem: Based on the findings of the Mundell-Fleming model, what is the best possible response to the candidate's Question 1?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Appreciation would follow restrictive monetary and/or expansionary fiscal policy; here both policies are expansionary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Depreciation would follow expansionary monetary and/or restrictive fiscal policy; here fiscal policy is expansionary, not restrictive.
explanations.C: Correct. Under high capital mobility with flexible exchange rates, the effect on the currency of monetary and fiscal policies that are both expansionary (or both restrictive) is indeterminate, because the monetary expansion pushes the currency down while the fiscal expansion pushes it up.

questions.los: Growth accounting: identify the largest contributor (capital vs labor vs TFP)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The labor contribution (1 - alpha)*labor growth = 0.4*1.3 = 0.52% is the smallest of the three.
explanations.B: Correct. Share of capital alpha = 0.6 (since labor share = 0.4). Capital contribution = alpha*capital growth = 0.6*6.2% = 3.72%; TFP = labor productivity growth - capital deepening = 3.4% - 1.7% = 1.7%; labor = 0.4*1.3% = 0.52%. Capital's 3.72% is the largest, so GDP growth is driven by capital.
explanations.C: Incorrect. TFP contributes 1.7%, less than the 3.72% from capital.

Max Busse is an analyst in the research department of a large
hedge fund. He was recently asked to develop a model to
predict the future exchange rate between two currencies.
Busse gathers monthly exchange rate data from the most
recent 10-year period and runs a regression based on the
following AR(1) model specification:
Regression 1: xt = b0 + b1xt-1 + εt, where xt is the exchange
rate at time t.
Based on his analysis of the time series and the regression
results, Busse reaches the following conclusions:
Conclusion 1: The variance of xt increases over time.
Conclusion 2: The mean-reverting level is undefined.
Conclusion 3: b0 does not appear to be significantly different
from 0. Busse decides to do additional analysis by first-
differencing the data and running a new regression.
Regression 2: Yt = b0 + b1Yt-1 + εt, where Yt = xt - xt-1.
Exhibit 1 shows the regression results.
Busse decides that he will need to test the data for
nonstationarity using a Dickey-Fuller test. To do so, he knows
he must model a transformed version of Regression 1.
Busse's next assignment is to develop a model to predict
future quarterly sales for PoweredUP, Inc., a major electronics
retailer. He begins by running the following regression:
Regression 3: ln Salest - ln Salest-1 = b0 + b1 (ln Salest-1 -ln
Salest-2) + εt.
Exhibit 2 presents the results of this regression.
Because the regression output from Exhibit 2 raises some
concerns, Busse runs a different regression. These regression
results, along with quarterly sales data for the past five
quarters, are presented in Exhibits 3 and 4, respectively.
After completing his work on PoweredUP, Busse is asked to
analyze the relationship of oil prices and the stock prices of
three transportation companies. His firm wants to know
whether the stock prices can be predicted by the price of oil.
Exhibit 5 shows selected information from the results of his
analysis.
To assess the relationship between oil prices and stock prices,
Busse runs three regressions using the time series of each
company's stock prices as the dependent variable and the
time series of oil prices as the independent variable.

questions.stem: Which of Busse's conclusions regarding the exchange rate time series is consistent with both the properties of a covariance-stationary time series and the properties of a random walk?
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
A random walk can be described by the equation xt = b0 +
b1xt-1 + εt, where b0 = 0 and b1 = 1. So b0 = 0 is a
characteristic of a random walk time series. A covariance-
stationary series must satisfy the following three
requirements:
1. The expected value of the time series must be constant and
finite in all periods.
2. The variance of the time series must be constant and finite
in all periods.
3. The covariance of the time series with itself for a fixed
number of periods in the past or future must be constant and
finite in all periods.
b0 = 0 does not violate any of these three requirements and is
thus consistent with the properties of a covariance-stationary
time series.

questions.stem: Based on the regression output in Exhibit 1, the first- differenced series used to run Regression 2 is consistent with:
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
The critical t-statistic at a 5% confidence level is 1.98. As a
result, neither the intercept nor the coefficient on the first lag
of the first-differenced exchange rate in Regression 2 differs
significantly from zero. Also, the residual autocorrelations do
not differ significantly from zero. As a result, Regression 2
can be reduced to yt = εt with a mean-reverting level of b0/(1
- b1) = 0/1 = 0. Therefore, the variance of yt in each period is
Var(εt) = σ2. The fact that the residuals are not
autocorrelated is consistent with the covariance of the times
series, with itself being constant and finite at different lags.
Because the variance and the mean of yt are constant and
finite in each period, we can also conclude that yt is
covariance stationary.

questions.stem: Based on the regression results in Exhibit 1, the original time series of exchange rates:

choices.C: can be modeled using linear regression.

questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
If the exchange rate series is a random walk, then the first-
differenced series will yield b0 = 0 and b1 = 0, and the error
terms will not be serially correlated. The data in Exhibit 1 show
that this is the case: Neither the intercept nor the coefficient
on the first lag of the first-differenced exchange rate in
Regression 2 differs significantly from zero because the t-
statistics of both coefficients are less than the critical t-
statistic of 1.98. Also, the residual autocorrelations do not
differ significantly from zero because the t-statistics of all
autocorrelations are less than the critical t-statistic of 1.98.
Therefore, because all random walks have unit roots, the
exchange rate time series used to run Regression 1 has a unit
root.

questions.stem: In order to perform the nonstationarity test, Busse should transform the Regression 1 equation by:

choices.A: adding the second lag to the equation.
choices.C: subtracting the independent variable from both sides of the equation.

questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
To conduct the Dickey-Fuller test, one must subtract the
independent variable, xt-1, from both sides of the original AR(1)
model. This results in a change of the dependent variable
(from xt to xt – xt-1) and a change in the regression's slope
coefficient (from b1 to b1 - 1) but not a change in the
independent variable.

questions.stem: Based on the regression output in Exhibit 2, what should lead Busse to conclude that the Regression 3 equation is not correctly specified?

choices.B: The t-statistic for the slope coefficient
choices.C: The t-statistics for the autocorrelations of the residual

The regression output in Exhibit 2 suggests there is serial
correlation in the residual errors. The fourth autocorrelation of

which is greater than the t-statistic critical value of 2.02.
Therefore, the null hypothesis that the fourth autocorrelation

Alef Associates manages a long-only fund specializing in
global smallcap equities. Since its founding a decade ago,
Alef maintains a portfolio of 100 stocks (out of an eligible
universe of about 10,000 stocks). Some of these holdings
are the result of screening the universe for attractive stocks
based on several ratios that use readily available market and
accounting data; others are the result of investment ideas
generated by Alef’s professional staff of five securities
analysts and two portfolio managers.
Although Alef’s investment performance has been good, its
Chief Investment Officer, Paul Moresanu, is contemplating a
change in the investment process aimed at achieving even
better returns. After attending multiple workshops and being
approached by data vendors, Moresanu feels that data
science should play a role in the way Alef selects its
investments. He has also noticed that much of Alef’s past
outperformance is due to stocks that became takeover
targets. After some research and reflection, Moresanu writes
the following email to the Alef’s CEO.
Subject: Investment Process Reorganization
I have been thinking about modernizing the way we select
stock investments. Given that our past success has put Alef
Associates in an excellent financial position, now seems to be
a good time to invest in our future. What I propose is that we
continue managing a portfolio of 100 global small-cap stocks
but restructure our process to benefit from machine learning
(ML). Importantly, the new process will still allow a role for
human insight, for example, in providing domain knowledge. In
addition, I think we should make a special effort to identify
companies that are likely to be acquired. Specifically, I suggest
following the four steps which would be repeated every
quarter.
Step 1 We apply ML techniques to a model including
fundamental and technical variables (features) to predict next
quarter’s return for each of the 100 stocks currently in our
portfolio. Then, the 20 stocks with the lowest estimated return
are identified for replacement.
Step 2 We utilize ML techniques to divide our investable
universe of about 10,000 stocks into 20 different groups,
based on a wide variety of the most relevant financial and
non-financial characteristics. The idea is to prevent
unintended portfolio concentration by selecting stocks from
each of these distinct groups.
Step 3 For each of the 20 different groups, we use labeled
data to train a model that will predict the five stocks (in any
given group) that are most likely to become acquisition
targets in the next one year.
Step 4 Our five experienced securities analysts are each
assigned four of the groups, and then each analyst selects
their one best stock pick from each of their assigned groups.
These 20 “high-conviction” stocks will be added to our
portfolio (in replacement of the 20 relatively underperforming
stocks to be sold in Step 1).
A couple of additional comments related to the
above:Comment 1 The ML algorithms will require large
amounts of data. We would first need to explore using free or
inexpensive historical datasets and then evaluate their
usefulness for the ML-based stock selection processes before
deciding on using data that requires subscription.Comment 2
As time passes, we expect to find additional ways to apply ML
techniques to refine Alef’s investment processes.What do
you think?
Paul Moresanu

questions.stem: Assuming a Classification and Regression Tree (CART) model is used to accomplish Step 3, which of the following is most likely to result in model overfitting?

questions.explanation:

Aaliyah Schultz is a fixed-income portfolio manager at Aries
Investments. Schultz supervises Ameris Steele, a junior
analyst.
A few years ago, Schultz developed a proprietary machine
learning (ML) model that aims to predict downgrades of
publicly-traded firms by bond rating agencies. The model
currently relies only on structured financial data collected
from different sources. Schultz thinks the model’s predictive
power may be improved by incorporating sentiment data
derived from textual analysis of news articles and Twitter
content relating to the subject companies.
Schultz and Steele meet to discuss plans for incorporating the
sentiment data into the model. They discuss the differences in
the steps between building ML models that use traditional
structured data and building ML models that use textual big
data. Steele tells Schultz:
Statement 1 The second step in building text-based ML
models is text preparation and wrangling, whereas the second
step in building ML models using structured data is data
collection.
Statement 2 The fourth step in building both types of models
encompasses data/text exploration.
Steele expresses concern about using Twitter content in the
model, noting that research suggests that as much as 10%–
15% of social media content is from fake accounts. Schultz
tells Steele that she understands her concern but thinks the
potential for model improvement outweighs the concern.
Steele begins building a model that combines the structured
financial data and the sentiment data. She starts with
cleansing and wrangling the raw structured financial data.
Exhibit 1 presents a small sample of the raw dataset before
cleansing: Each row represents data for a particular firm.
After cleansing the data, Steele then preprocesses the
dataset. She creates two new variables: an “Age” variable
based on the firm’s IPO date and an “Interest Coverage
Ratio” variable equal to EBIT divided by interest expense. She
also deletes the “IPO Date” variable from the dataset. After
applying these transformations, Steele scales the financial
data using normalization. She notes that over the full sample
dataset, the “Interest Expense” variable ranges from a
minimum of 0.2 and a maximum of 12.2, with a mean of 1.1
and a standard deviation of 0.4.
Steele and Schultz then discuss how to preprocess the raw
text data. Steele tells Schultz that the process can be
completed in the following three steps:
Step 1 Cleanse the raw text data.
Step 2 Split the cleansed data into a collection of words for
them to be normalized.
Step 3 Normalize the collection of words from Step 2 and
create a distinct set of tokens from the normalized words.
With respect to Step 1, Steele tells Schultz:
“I believe I should remove all html tags, punctuations,
numbers, and extra white spaces from the data before
normalizing them.”
After properly cleansing the raw text data, Steele completes
Steps 2 and 3. She then performs exploratory data analysis.
To assist in feature selection, she wants to create a
visualization that shows the most informative words in the
dataset based on their term frequency (TF) values. After
creating and analyzing the visualization, Steele is concerned
that some tokens are likely to be noise features for ML model
training; therefore, she wants to remove them.
Steele and Schultz discuss the importance of feature selection
and feature engineering in ML model training. Steele tells
Schultz:
“Appropriate feature selection is a key factor in minimizing
model overfitting, whereas feature engineering tends to
prevent model underfitting.”
Once satisfied with the final set of features, Steele selects and
runs a model on the training set that classifies the text as
having positive sentiment (Class “1” or negative sentiment
(Class “0”). She then evaluates its performance using error
analysis. The resulting confusion matrix is presented in Exhibit
2.

questions.stem: Given her objective, the visualization that Steele should create in the exploratory data analysis step is a:
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
Steele wants to create a visualization for Schultz that shows
the most informative words in the dataset based on their term
frequency (TF, the ratio of the number of times a given token
occurs in the dataset to the total number of tokens in the
dataset) values. A word cloud is a common visual-ization when
working with text data as it can be made to visualize the most

questions.stem: To address her concern in her exploratory data analysis, Steele should focus on those tokens that have:

choices.C: very low and very high term frequency (TF) values.

questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
Frequency measures can be used for vocabulary pruning to
remove noise features by filtering the tokens with very high
and low TF values across all the texts. Noise features are both
the most frequent and most sparse (or rare) tokens in the
dataset. On one end, noise features can be stop words that
are typically present frequently in all the texts across the
dataset. On the other end, noise features can be sparse terms
that are present in only a few text files. Text classification
involves dividing text documents into assigned classes. The
frequent tokens strain the ML model to choose a decision
boundary among the texts as the terms are present across all
the texts (an example of underfitting). The rare tokens mislead
the ML model into classifying texts containing the rare terms
into a specific class (an example of overfitting). Thus,
identifying and removing noise features are critical steps for
text classification applications.

questions.stem: Is Steele’s statement regarding the relationship between feature selection/feature engineering and model fit correct?

choices.B: No, because she is incorrect with respect to feature selection.
choices.C: No, because she is incorrect with respect to feature engineering.

questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
A dataset with a small number of features may not carry all
the characteristics that explain relationships between the
target variable and the features. Conversely, a large number
of features can complicate the model and potentially distort
patterns in the data due to low degrees of freedom, causing
overfitting. Therefore, appropriate feature selection is a key
factor in minimizing such model overfitting. Feature
engineering tends to prevent underfitting in the training of the
model. New features, when engineered properly, can elevate
the underlying data points that better explain the interactions
of features. Thus, feature engineering can be critical to
overcome underfitting.

questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the model’s precision metric is closest to:
questions.explanation:

Precision, the ratio of correctly predicted positive classes
(true positives) to all predicted positive classes, is calculated
as: Precision (P) = TP/(TP＋FP) = 182/(182＋52) = 0.7778
(78%).

questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the model’s F1 score is closest to:
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
The model’s F1 score, which is the harmonic mean of
precision and recall, is calculated as:
F1 score = (2 × P × R)/(P＋R).
F1 score = (2 × 0.7778 × 0.8545)/(0.7778＋0.8545) =
0.8143 (81%).

questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the model’s accuracy metric is closest to:
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
The model’s accuracy, which is the percentage of correctly
predicted classes out of total predictions, is calculated as:
Accuracy = (TP＋TN)/(TP＋FP＋TN＋FN).
Accuracy = (182＋96)/(182＋52＋96＋31) = 0.7701 (77%).

Iesha Azarov is a senior analyst at Ganymede Moon Partners
(Ganymede), where he works with junior analyst Pàola Bector.
Azarov would like to incorporate machine learning (ML)
models into the company’s analytical process. Azarov asks
Bector to develop ML models for two unstructured stock
sentiment datasets, Dataset ABC and Dataset XYZ. Both
datasets have been cleaned and preprocessed in preparation
for text exploration and model training.
Following an exploratory data analysis that revealed Dataset
ABC’s most frequent tokens, Bector conducts a collection
frequency analysis. Bector then computes TF–IDF (term
frequency–inverse document frequency) for several words in
the collection and tells Azarov the following:
Statement 1: IDF is equal to the inverse of the document
frequency measure.
Statement 2: TF at the collection level is multiplied by IDF to
calculate TF–IDF.
Statement 3: TF–IDF values vary by the number of
documents in the dataset, and therefore, model performance
can vary when applied to a dataset with just a few documents.
Bector notes that Dataset ABC is characterized by the
absence of ground truth.
Bector turns his attention to Dataset XYZ, containing 84,000
tokens and 10,000 sentences. Bector chooses an appropriate
feature selection method to identify and remove unnecessary
tokens from the dataset and then focuses on model training.
For performance evaluation purposes, Dataset XYZ is split
into a training set, cross-validation (CV) set, and test set. Each
of the sentences has already been labeled as either a positive
sentiment (Class “1”) or a negative sentiment (Class “0”)
sentence. There is an unequal class distribution between the
positive sentiment and negative sentiment sentences in
Dataset XYZ. Simple random sampling is applied within levels
of the sentiment class labels to balance the class distributions
within the splits. Bector’s view is that the false positive and
false negative evaluation metrics should be given equal weight.
Select performance data from the cross-validation set
confusion matrices is presented in Exhibit 1:
Azarov and Bector evaluate the Dataset XYZ performance
metrics for Confusion Matrices A, B, and C in Exhibit 1. Azarov
says, “For Ganymede’s purposes, we should be most
concerned with the cost of Type I errors.”
Azarov requests that Bector apply the ML model to the test
dataset for Dataset XYZ, assuming a threshold p-value of
0.65. Exhibit 2 contains a sample of results from the test
dataset corpus.
Bector makes the following remarks regarding model training:
Remark 1: Method selection is governed by such factors as
the type of data and the size of data.
Remark 2: In the performance evaluation stage, model fitting
errors, such as bias error and variance error, are used to
measure goodness of fit.

questions.stem: Based on the text exploration method used for Dataset ABC, tokens that potentially carry important information useful for differentiating the sentiment embedded in the text are most likely to have values that are:

解析
When analyzing term frequency at the corpus level, also

frequency (TF) values potentially carry important information
useful for differentiating the sentiment embedded in the text.
Tokens with the highest TF values are mostly stop words that
do not contribute to differentiating the sentiment embedded
in the text, and tokens with the lowest TF values are mostly

not important to the meaning of the text.
C is incorrect because tokens with the highest TF values are
mostly stop words (noisy terms) that do not contribute to

Statement 3 is correct. TF–IDF values vary by the number of
documents in the dataset, and therefore, the model
performance can vary when applied to a dataset with just a
few documents. Statement 1 is incorrect because IDF is
calculated as the log of the inverse, or reciprocal, of the
document frequency measure. Statement 2 is incorrect
because TF at the sentence (not collection) level is multiplied

questions.stem: What percentage of Dataset ABC should be allocated to a training subset?
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
0% of the master dataset of Dataset ABC should be allocated
to a training subset. Dataset ABC is characterized by the
absence of ground truth (i.e., no known outcome or target
variable) and is therefore an unsupervised ML model. For
unsupervised learning models, no splitting of the master
dataset is needed, because of the absence of labeled training
data. Supervised ML datasets (with labeled training data)
contain ground truth, the known outcome (target variable) of
each observation in the dataset.
B is incorrect because 20% is the commonly recommended
split for the cross-validation set and test set in supervised
training ML datasets. Dataset ABC is an unsupervised ML
dataset, for which no splitting (0%) of the master dataset is
needed, because of the absence of labeled training data. In
supervised ML models (which contain labeled training data),
the master dataset is split into three subsets (a training set,
cross-validation set, and test set), which are used for model
training and testing purposes.
C is incorrect because 60% is the commonly recommended
split for the training set in supervised training ML datasets.
Dataset ABC is an unsupervised ML dataset, for which no
splitting (0%) of the master dataset is needed, because of the
absence of labeled training data. In supervised ML models
(which contain labeled training data), the master dataset is
split into three subsets (a training set, cross-validation set, and
test set), which are used for model training and testing
purposes.

questions.stem: Based only on Dataset XYZ’s composition and Bector’s view regarding false positive and false negative evaluation metrics, which performance measure is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
F1 score is the most appropriate performance measure for
Dataset XYZ. Bector gives equal weight to false positives and
false negatives. Accuracy and F1 score are overall
performance measures that give equal weight to false
positives and false negatives. Accuracy is considered an
appropriate performance measure for balanced datasets,
where the number of “1” and “0” classes are equal. F1
score is considered more appropriate than accuracy when
there is unequal class distribution in the dataset and it is
necessary to measure the equilibrium of precision and recall.
Since Dataset XYZ contains an unequal class distribution
between positive and negative sentiment sentences, F1 score
is the most appropriate performance measure.
Precision is the ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to
all predicted positive classes and is useful in situations where
the cost of false positives or Type I errors is high. Recall is the
ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to all actual
positive classes and is useful in situations where the cost of
false negatives or Type II errors is high.
A is incorrect because Bector gives equal weight to false
positives and false negatives. Accuracy and F1 score are
overall performance measures that give equal weight to false
positives and false negatives. Recall is the ratio of correctly
predicted positive classes to all actual positive classes and is
useful in situations where the cost of false negatives or Type II
errors is high.
C is incorrect because Bector gives equal weight to false
positive and false negatives. Accuracy and F1 score are
overall performance measures that give equal weight to false
positives and false negatives. Precision is the ratio of correctly
predicted positive classes to all predicted positive classes and
is useful in situations where the cost of false positives or
Type-I error is high.

questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, which confusion matrix demonstrates the most favorable value of the performance metric that best addresses Azarov’s concern?
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
Precision is the ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to
all predicted positive classes and is useful in situations where
the cost of false positives or Type I errors is high. Confusion
Matrix A has the highest precision and therefore
demonstrates the most favorable value of the performance
metric that best addresses Azarov’s concern about the cost
of Type I errors. Confusion Matrix A has a precision score of
0.95, which is higher than the precision scores of Confusion
Matrix B (0.93) and Confusion Matrix C (0.86).
B is incorrect because precision, not accuracy, is the
performance measure that best addresses Azarov’s concern
about the cost of Type I errors. Confusion Matrix B
demonstrates the most favorable value for the accuracy score
(0.92), which is higher than the accuracy scores of Confusion
Matrix A (0.91) and Confusion Matrix C (0.91). Accuracy is a
performance measure that gives equal weight to false
positives and false negatives and is considered an appropriate
performance measure when the class distribution in the
dataset is equal (a balanced dataset). However, Azarov is most
concerned with the cost of false positives, or Type I errors,
and not with finding the equilibrium between precision and
recall. Furthermore, Dataset XYZ has an unequal (unbalanced)
class distribution between positive sentiment and negative
sentiment sentences.
C is incorrect because precision, not recall or F1 score, is the
performance measure that best addresses Azarov’s concern
about the cost of Type I errors. Confusion Matrix C
demonstrates the most favorable value for the recall score
(0.97), which is higher than the recall scores of Confusion
Matrix A (0.87) and Confusion Matrix B (0.90). Recall is the
ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to all actual
positive classes and is useful in situations where the cost of
false negatives, or Type II errors, is high. However, Azarov is
most concerned with the cost of Type I errors, not Type II
errors.
F1 score is more appropriate (than accuracy) when there is
unequal class distribution in the dataset and it is necessary to
measure the equilibrium of precision and recall. Confusion
Matrix C demonstrates the most favorable value for the F1
score (0.92), which is higher than the F1 scores of Confusion
Matrix A (0.91) and Confusion Matrix B (0.91). Although
Dataset XYZ has an unequal class distribution between
positive sentiment and negative sentiment sentences, Azarov
is most concerned with the cost of false positives, or Type I
errors, and not with finding the equilibrium between precision
and recall.

questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the accuracy metric for Dataset XYZ’s test set sample is closest to:
questions.explanation:
一般推荐：
解析
Accuracy is the percentage of correctly predicted classes out
of total predictions and is calculated as (TP + TN)/(TP + FP +
TN + FN). In order to obtain the values for true positive (TP),
true negative (TN), false positive (FP), and false negative (FN),
predicted sentiment for the positive (Class “1”) and the
negative (Class “0”) classes are determined based on
whether each individual target p-value is greater than or less
than the threshold p-value of 0.65. If an individual target p-
value is greater than the threshold p-value of 0.65, the
predicted sentiment for that instance is positive (Class “1”).
If an individual target p-value is less than the threshold p-value
of 0.65, the predicted sentiment for that instance is negative
(Class “0”). Actual sentiment and predicted sentiment are
then classified as follows:
Exhibit 2, with added “Predicted Sentiment” and
“Classification” columns, is presented below:
Based on the classification data obtained from Exhibit 2, a
confusion matrix can be generated:
Using the data in the confusion matrix above, the accuracy
metric is computed as follows:Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + FP
+ TN + FN).Accuracy = (3 + 4)/(3 + 1 + 4 + 2) = 0.70.A is
incorrect because 0.67 is the F1 score, not accuracy metric,
for the sample of the test set for Dataset XYZ, based on
Exhibit 2. To calculate the F1 score, the precision (P) and the
recall (R) ratios must first be calculated. Precision and recall
for the sample of the test set for Dataset XYZ, based on
Exhibit 2, are calculated as follows:Precision (P) = TP/(TP +
FP) = 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75.Recall (R) = TP/(TP + FN) = 3/(3 + 2) =
0.60.The F1 score is calculated as follows:F1 score = (2 × P
× R)/(P + R) = (2 × 0.75 × 0.60)/(0.75 + 0.60) = 0.667, or
0.67.C is incorrect because 0.75 is the precision ratio, not the
accuracy metric, for the sample of the test set for Dataset
